cells.tense: What you're building is getting your hands on it right now, and you're choosing what it needs next.
cells.ask: When something you tend finishes what it was for, let it be done — say the work is complete, and hand the next thing your care.
cells.core:
You're giving what you're growing exactly what it needs, when it needs it, and your direction holds because you're tending it instead of dragging it. Nothing gets forced and nothing gets dropped. You know the difference between a thing that wants more time and a thing that's asking to be moved along, and you keep the whole enterprise moving without burning yourself down to do it.

That steadiness is the whole of it. What you're cultivating gets your attention and stays in your hands, and because you're not clutching it, it can actually grow. When a thing you've tended reaches its end, you don't have to fight that. You can set it down finished and turn to what's next, and the turning is not a loss. It's what the care was for all along.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's growing and keep your direction, and you know when a thing is finished.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady hands, giving it what it needs to hold
cells.place: the work of moving toward something, keeping your direction through resistance without being eaten by it

cells.tense: You're standing ahead of a harvest that hasn't come in yet, tending a crop on land you don't own, bracing for a season you keep trying to start early.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're tending that someone else could carry, and set it down for a week — let what you've already made be enough to want from.
cells.core:
You're working hard at what you're growing and watching it like a hawk. The tending itself is good — you give what's needed, you keep the direction, you hold what depends on you. But you want it to be abundant, to satisfy what you imagined, so you tend it past the point where it wants to be tended. You're reaching into a future you can't harvest yet, and the reaching is pulling you out of the one you're standing in.

The direction is still there. What's slipping is trust that what you've made so far is real. Roots don't grow faster when you dig them up to check. When you can let the work be enough as it is, the wanting itself softens, and you find you're already standing in something finished enough to enjoy.
cells.sheetLine: You keep tending toward a harvest that hasn't come, and the work is wearing you thin.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady hands, giving it what it needs to hold
cells.place: the work of moving toward something, keeping your direction through resistance without being eaten by it

cells.tense: You set the tools down a while back, and you're still standing in the field you used to work.
cells.ask: Put one small thing back in your hands this week — something unfinished you can tend for a few minutes, and let the tending be the point.
cells.core:
You know how to tend what's growing. You know how to hold a direction and keep giving it what it needs. That's not gone — it's the part of you that still knows how to keep a thing alive without forcing it, and it's how you got anything that's still standing around you.

What stopped is the giving. You're not moving toward anything right now, and you're not tending a thing you could name. You're parked where the last harvest used to be, and you're not sure it's yours to start again. It is. Nothing has to be decided about the whole field today. Something small, held in your hands for a few minutes, until the tending itself reminds you it's still yours to do.
cells.sheetLine: The tools are down and you're still standing in the field.
cells.verb: tending what's growing with steady hands, giving it what it needs to hold
cells.place: the work of moving toward something, keeping your direction through resistance without being eaten by it

cells.tense: Your hands are already in the work, tending what needs tending and moving toward what you want, but you're talking about it like it's just happening to you.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you're holding together and why it matters to you, out loud, and let them hear it was your choice.
cells.core:
You tend what's growing every day. You keep the direction, you give what's needed, you hold the things that depend on you — and you do it quietly, as if the work were just the shape things take on their own. The care is real and the results show it, and you keep the whole thing moving without a fuss.

The tending is real and it's yours. What's missing is you saying so — to someone, once, without dressing it up as obligation or accident. Being acknowledged isn't a reward you're owed; it's the completion of the thing itself. When you name what you've carried and why, the work gets to be finished in the open, and you get to set it down as something you did.
cells.sheetLine: You're doing the tending. You just haven't claimed it as yours.
